domains: 18 population-genetics + 3 Turing math-domain Delphi records (Thompson's 71 math-bearing records are NOT included)
global_limits: Source-correspondence of each record to the original paper is NOT reviewed.
Statuses and 'does not establish' text are the critic's single-reader judgement (not computed).
Codex has not approved this scorecard; 'Codex-reviewed' refers to the cited artifacts only.
All checks are of DECLARED models (bench conventions, Lean statements); nothing here validates any biological claim; the host's B0-B3 buckets are not used.
Delphi LLM assessments are not used as evidence (0 assessments present in these records).

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: An advantageous allele spreading through a continuous population advances as a travelling wave whose speed is set by the selection coefficient and the diffusion (dispersal) rate.
rows.label: Fisher-KPP wave of advance of an advantageous gene
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Ronald A. Fisher (1937) The wave of advance of advantageous genes
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: u_t = D u_{xx} + s u(1-u); travelling waves u(x-ct) exist iff c \ge c^* = 2\sqrt{sD}; compactly supported initial data spread at asymptotic speed c^*
rows.record_context: Assumptions: one spatial dimension (extended to R^n), constant diffusion D, logistic (genic) selection with coefficient s, deterministic large-population limit. Formal status: proved; Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov (1937) gave the proof independently, and Aronson and Weinberger (1978) proved the asymptotic spreading speed in several dimensions. Finite populations, Allee effects or long-tailed dispersal change the speed.

evidence.evidence: scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key.jsonl (family fisher_kpp_speed, 16 items)
scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key_verification.json (independent finite-difference front speeds: logistic ~2, pushed cubic alpha=10/3: 2.062 vs analytic 2.066; Allee 0.2817 vs 0.2828)

rows.scope_finding: The speed 2*sqrt(sD) is the pulled-front speed for KPP growth; for a strong-Allee (bistable) term the front is pushed and slower, and for u(1-u)(1+alpha u) it holds iff alpha<=2 (Hadeler-Rothe); the exact-KPP inequality f(u)<=f'(0)u fails for 1<alpha<=2 although the speed still holds (benign items).
rows.does_not_establish: Declared reaction terms on the line with wide initial data; the minimal-speed theorem was cited (Crooks-Grinfeld 2020), not reproved; PDE speeds are finite-time estimates.

Status wording: no.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.
rows.label: Hamilton's rule
rows.source_point2_dct_source: W. D. Hamilton (1964) The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: \Delta \bar{p} > 0 \iff r b - c > 0, with r, b, c defined as regression coefficients (Queller form via the Price equation)
rows.record_context: Assumptions: in Hamilton's original derivation, additive fitness effects and weak selection; in the general form, b and c are partial regressions of fitness on the actor's and the partner's genotype. Formal status: proved; exact in the regression form (Gardner, West and Wild 2011). Critics argue that the general form is close to an identity with little predictive content (Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson 2010).

evidence.evidence: scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key.jsonl (family hamilton_rule_form, 16 items)
lean_price/Price.lean (queller, hamilton_form; README with prior-art correction; commit e776030)
experiments/price_probe/ on work/codex-api (Codex's own Price/Hamilton probe; separate artifact)

rows.scope_finding: The sign of rb-c equals the sign of the selection covariance exactly when w is exactly linear in own and partner genotype with an orthogonal residual (regression form, which the record's context names); with an interaction (synergy) term and the additive b,c the rule can have the wrong sign (bench witnesses). The record states both readings, so this is an ambiguity the textbook form hides, not a fault in the record.
rows.does_not_establish: Haploid pairing model with Malthusian payoffs and a stated pairing kernel; the one-way/algebraic statement only; no claim about real populations or about the generality debate (Nowak et al. 2010 vs Gardner et al. 2011). Price/Queller algebra duplicates existing formalization (atlas-lean Selection.lean has Price); our Queller-form corollary was not found there (code search, not exhaustive).

Lean node: lean_price reviewed by the critic only; Codex's separate price_probe is its own work. Status wording: no.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.
rows.label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Motoo Kimura (1962) On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: u(p) = \frac{1-e^{-4N_e s p}}{1-e^{-4N_e s}}; neutral limit u(p) = p, so a new mutant fixes with probability 1/(2N)
rows.record_context: Assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, genic (additive) selection with coefficient s, constant effective size N_e, no linkage to other selected sites. Formal status: proved within the diffusion limit.

evidence.evidence: scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key.jsonl (family kimura_regime, 16 items)
scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key_verification.json (power-iteration of the exact haploid Wright-Fisher chain)

rows.scope_finding: The record's diffusion formula and its neutral limit 1/N are approximations: within a 10% criterion against the exact haploid Wright-Fisher one-copy fixation probability, the neutral value fails when Ns is not small and the diffusion formula fails at small N with large s (bench witnesses).
rows.does_not_establish: Haploid WF chain with binomial sampling after selection (the record concerns the diploid diffusion setting); 10% is a declared tolerance. facebookresearch/atlas-lean (MathlibExt/Biology/PopulationGenetics/Diffusion/KimuraFixationProcess.lean) formalizes related Kimura material; we did not compare statements.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: A homogeneous steady state of two reacting chemicals that is stable without diffusion can become unstable to spatial perturbations when the chemicals diffuse at different rates, spontaneously producing a pattern.
rows.label: Turing diffusion-driven instability
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Alan Turing (1952) The chemical basis of morphogenesis
rows.math_point7_skos_notation:
u_t = f(u,v) + D_u 
abla^2 u, v_t = g(u,v) + D_v 
abla^2 v; with tr J < 0 and det J > 0, instability at some wavenumber k iff D_v f_u + D_u g_v > 2\sqrt{D_u D_v \det J}, which requires D_u 
e D_v
rows.record_context: Assumptions: two species, smooth kinetics, linearization about a homogeneous steady state, fixed domain without growth or mechanics. Formal status: the linear instability conditions are proved; existence and stability of nonlinear patterns are proved for many specific models but not in general.

evidence.evidence: scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key.jsonl (families turing_finite_domain 21 items, turing_2d_rectangle 15)
turing_scope/examples/short_L_pi.json (J=[[1,-2],[2,-3]], Du=1, Dv=10: continuum band 1/5<q<1/2 non-empty, no admissible Neumann mode at L=pi; mode appears at L=2pi)
turing_scope/lean/Audit.lean (+ docs/turing-scope.md): integer-model determinant/trace and mode-tail algebra, mutants
scopedesk/bench/audit/oracle_layer_audit_v1_2.json (NCA oracle 50/50 incl. these families)

rows.scope_finding: The record's textbook inequality is a continuum statement; on a finite domain with a stated boundary type only the admissible modes count, so a system can satisfy the inequality and have no growing mode (witness above), and mode sets differ between Neumann, Dirichlet and periodic boundaries and between 1-D and 2-D domains (bench witnesses).
rows.does_not_establish: Linear stability of a DECLARED two-species Jacobian only; no nonlinear pattern, no biology, no PDE theorem (Lean covers the integer algebra, not the equivalence with the PDE). Finite-domain mode quantisation is classical (textbook-derivable), so this is not a discovery. The record's own text names no boundary condition or domain shape (those are additions listed by the oracle's gate).

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: The spacing of a Turing pattern at onset is set by the reaction rates and diffusivities, not by the size of the tissue, so changing these parameters predictably changes the number of repeated elements.
rows.label: Turing wavelength selection
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Alan Turing (1952) The chemical basis of morphogenesis
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: at onset k_c^2 = \sqrt{\det J/(D_u D_v)}, \lambda_c = 2\pi/k_c; under uniform rescaling of D, \lambda \propto \sqrt{D}
rows.record_context: Assumptions: near onset of instability, two species, domain large compared with the wavelength. Formal status: proved by linear analysis. Away from onset, the selected wavelength depends on nonlinear terms and history.

evidence.evidence: scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key.jsonl (family wavelength_formula_licence, 14 items)
scopedesk/oracles gate.wavelength_licence audit: scopedesk/bench/audit/oracle_layer_audit_v1_2.json

rows.scope_finding: lambda_c = 2*pi/k_c is not the wavelength of the fastest-growing ADMISSIBLE mode on a finite domain: the bench items show cases where the two differ by more than 10% (near-onset and large-domain conditions in the record are qualitative; the 10% tolerance is the benchmark's declared operationalisation).
rows.does_not_establish: Linear fastest-growing mode only (no nonlinear selection, which the NCA study found to differ from the linear prediction in many cases); the 10% threshold and the 'fastest-growing = largest real part' convention are ours; five boundary/length-notation wording issues are disclosed in FROZEN.md.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.
rows.label: Hawk-Dove mixed ESS
rows.source_point2_dct_source: John Maynard Smith (1982) Evolution and the Theory of Games
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: payoffs E(H,H) = (V-C)/2, E(H,D) = V, E(D,H) = 0, E(D,D) = V/2; for C > V the unique ESS plays Hawk with probability p^* = V/C
rows.record_context: Assumptions: symmetric pairwise contests, fixed V and C, no role asymmetries (asymmetries such as ownership give the Bourgeois ESS instead). Formal status: proved within the game.

evidence.evidence: scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key.jsonl (family hawk_dove_ess, 16 items)
scopedesk/bench/v1_2/key_verification.json (replicator-dynamics check)

rows.does_not_establish: Exact check (E(p*,q)-E(q,q)=(C/2)(p*-q)^2>0) that for C>V the mixed strategy p*=V/C is an ESS and that for C<V p*>1 is not a probability (the record's own 'C > V' scope); the payoff matrix is the one stated in the convention text. Not established: anything beyond the symmetric two-strategy game, finite populations, or biology.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: The rate of increase in mean fitness of a population due to natural selection equals its additive genetic variance in fitness at that time.
rows.label: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection (partial-change form)
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Ronald A. Fisher (1930) The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: \Delta_{NS}\bar{w} = V_A(w)/\bar{w} (discrete generations); \left.\frac{d\bar{m}}{dt}\right|_{NS} = V_A(m) for Malthusian fitness m
rows.record_context: Assumptions: the 'partial change' holds average effects of alleles and the environment fixed (Price 1972, Ewens 1989); V_A is the additive genetic variance in fitness. Formal status: proved in this partial-change reading. Read as a claim about the total change in mean fitness it is false under dominance, epistasis, frequency dependence or a changing environment.

evidence.evidence: lean_price/Price.lean (Price identity; the z=w case gives Var(w) but is not stated as a separate theorem)
facebookresearch/atlas-lean MathlibExt/Biology/PopulationGenetics/Selection.lean (Price + Fisher FTNS in the exact haploid form) - existing work, not ours
experiments/price_probe/ on work/codex-api (Codex: fitness_selection is total-variance selection, NOT additive-genetic Fisher FTNS)

rows.does_not_establish: Only the Price-identity algebra (selection term = covariance with fitness) is machine-checked, with standard axioms and two failing mutants. The record's statement is about ADDITIVE genetic variance and 'partial change'; that partition (and any diploid, multilocus or epistatic setting) is NOT formalized by us. Our Price node duplicates atlas-lean's. No scope-failure was exhibited by a bench family for this record.
rows.codex_reviewed: Price probe by Codex is separate; Codex's price-target review: planning/rethink/CODEX-21-CLAIM-FREEZE-REVIEW.md and price_probe README. Status wording: no.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.
rows.label: Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Motoo Kimura (1968) Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: empirical claim: for most sites |N_e s| \lesssim 1, so the fraction of substitutions driven by positive selection \alpha is small; tested with d_N/d_S and McDonald-Kreitman \alpha = 1 - \frac{D_s P_n}{D_n P_s}
rows.record_context: Formal status: not a mathematical statement; an empirical claim about the distribution of fitness effects. King and Jukes (1969) proposed it independently. Genomic estimates of alpha and pervasive linked selection are cited against its strong form (Kern and Hahn 2018).

evidence.evidence: records/kimura-neutral-theory.json (delphi:hypothesisType empirical-law; context: 'not a mathematical statement; an empirical claim')

rows.does_not_establish: Nothing is checked; the record declares an empirical claim tested with dN/dS.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: Chemical substances that react and diffuse through tissue (morphogens) are sufficient to account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.
rows.label: Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Alan Turing (1952) The chemical basis of morphogenesis
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: no canonical formalization: the claim asserts that a biological pattern is generated by a system of the form u_t = F(u) + D\nabla^2 u with D not proportional to the identity
rows.record_context: Formal status: a framework rather than a mathematical proposition. Kondo and Asai (1995) confirmed the predicted stripe-branching dynamics in Pomacanthus and Castets et al. (1990) produced Turing patterns chemically. Mechanical buckling, prepatterns and cell-cell signalling can produce the same patterns, so a matching pattern alone does not identify the mechanism.

evidence.evidence: records/turing-morphogen-hypothesis.json (delphi:hypothesisType principle-or-framework; context: 'a framework rather than a mathematical proposition')

rows.does_not_establish: Nothing is checked. The record declares itself a framework with no canonical formalisation.

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: Continuous traits determined by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect produce the observed correlations between relatives, so biometric and Mendelian inheritance are consistent.
rows.label: Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Ronald A. Fisher (1919) The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: Cov(z_i, z_j) = 2\Theta_{ij} V_A + \Delta_{ij} V_D; in the limit of M \to \infty loci the offspring trait given parents is Gaussian with mean (z_1+z_2)/2 and segregation variance V_0(1-\bar{F}), with error O(1/\sqrt{M}) (Barton, Etheridge and Veber 2017)
rows.record_context: Assumptions: many unlinked loci of small additive effect, random mating, environmental effects independent of genotype. Formal status: the covariance decomposition is proved; the infinitesimal limit, including under selection, is proved by Barton, Etheridge and Veber (2017). Large-effect loci and epistasis break the Gaussian limit.
rows.does_not_establish: no bench family, oracle or Lean node attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: Under random mating and autosomal inheritance, selection drives parents to invest equally in sons and daughters, which gives a 1:1 sex ratio when the two cost the same.
rows.label: Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Ronald A. Fisher (1930) The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: ESS allocation: N_m c_m = N_f c_f; with c_m = c_f the unbeatable primary sex ratio is 1:1
rows.record_context: Assumptions: panmixia, autosomal control of the sex ratio, each offspring has one father and one mother, no local mate competition or sex-specific resource competition. Formal status: proved as an invasion (ESS) result (Shaw and Mohler 1953). Its own named exceptions (local mate competition, Hamilton 1967) are predicted deviations, not refutations.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.
rows.label: Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
rows.source_point2_dct_source: W. D. Hamilton (1964) The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: with a singly mated queen, r_{sister,sister} = 3/4 > r_{mother,daughter} = 1/2, but r_{sister,brother} = 1/4
rows.record_context: Formal status: the relatedness coefficients are proved. The explanatory claim is largely abandoned: the low sister-brother relatedness offsets the gain unless the sex ratio is biased, diploid termites are eusocial, and comparative work points to ancestral monogamy instead (Hughes et al. 2008).
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted (record typed 'conjecture'; relatedness coefficients are stated as proved)

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.
rows.label: Local mate competition sex ratio
rows.source_point2_dct_source: W. D. Hamilton (1967) Extraordinary Sex Ratios
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: unbeatable proportion of males x^* = \frac{n-1}{2n} for n foundresses per patch (diploid case)
rows.record_context: Assumptions: n foundresses per patch, mating confined to the natal patch, only females disperse, mothers control the sex ratio. Formal status: proved as an ESS within the model. Haplodiploidy and inbreeding shift x* slightly.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.
rows.label: Declining force of selection with age
rows.source_point2_dct_source: W. D. Hamilton (1966) The moulding of senescence by natural selection
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: s(a) = \frac{\partial r}{\partial \ln p_a} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{x=a+1}^{\infty} e^{-rx} l_x m_x, non-increasing in a
rows.record_context: Assumptions: an age-structured population with fixed age-specific fertility and no growth or repair after maturity. Formal status: the formula for s(a) is proved. The inevitability claim is refuted as stated: Jones et al. (2013) found species with flat or declining mortality with age, consistent with life histories where fertility rises with size.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.
rows.label: Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Motoo Kimura (1969) The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: \bar{t}_1(p) = -\frac{4N_e(1-p)\ln(1-p)}{p}; as p = 1/(2N) \to 0, \bar{t}_1 \to 4N_e generations
rows.record_context: Assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, neutrality, constant N_e. Formal status: proved within the diffusion limit (Kimura and Ohta 1969).
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted (the bench's kimura_regime family tests the fixation PROBABILITY only)

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.
rows.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Motoo Kimura (1964) The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: H = \frac{\theta}{1+\theta}, \theta = 4N_e\mu (infinite-alleles model)
rows.record_context: Assumptions: infinite-alleles mutation, neutrality, constant N_e, equilibrium. Formal status: proved within the model. Observed diversity varies far less across species than census sizes predict (Lewontin's paradox; Leffler et al. 2012), which points to linked selection and demography.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.
rows.label: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate
rows.source_point2_dct_source: Motoo Kimura (1968) Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: k = 2N\mu \cdot \frac{1}{2N} = \mu
rows.record_context: Assumptions: strictly neutral mutations, mutation rate constant per generation, steady state. Formal status: an exact consequence of the neutral fixation probability. Variation in generation time and weak selection on nearly neutral sites cause departures from strict clock-like rates.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted (k=mu arithmetic; trivial but not checked)

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
rows.label: Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions
rows.source_point2_dct_source: John Maynard Smith (1973) The Logic of Animal Conflict
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: I is an ESS iff for all J \ne I: E(I,I) > E(J,I), or E(I,I) = E(J,I) and E(I,J) > E(J,J); every ESS is an asymptotically stable rest point of the replicator dynamics (Taylor and Jonker 1978), not conversely
rows.record_context: Assumptions: an infinite, well-mixed population with pairwise interactions and asexual or clonal inheritance of strategies. Formal status: the definition is exact, and the link to replicator dynamics is proved. Finite populations, mutation and genetic constraints can stop an ESS from being reached.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted (general ESS definition; only the Hawk-Dove instance is checked)

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.
rows.label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
rows.source_point2_dct_source: John Maynard Smith (1974) The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: the relative heterozygosity H_{after}/H_{before} at a neutral site at recombination fraction c is an increasing function of c/s that tends to 0 as c/s \to 0; the affected region has a width of order s in recombination units, up to logarithmic factors in N
rows.record_context: Assumptions: a single sweep from a new mutation, deterministic allele-frequency trajectory, two loci. Formal status: proved under these approximations (later refined in coalescent treatments). Background selection produces a similar correlation between diversity and recombination.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.
rows.label: Twofold cost of sex
rows.source_point2_dct_source: John Maynard Smith (1978) The Evolution of Sex
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: with equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio, the odds of asexual to sexual females double each generation: \frac{q_{t+1}}{1-q_{t+1}} = 2\frac{q_t}{1-q_t}
rows.record_context: Assumptions: anisogamy with males contributing no resources, equal fecundity and viability of sexual and asexual females, a 1:1 sex ratio. Formal status: proved as a population-dynamic identity under these assumptions. Its biological force depends on how often those assumptions hold.
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted

rows.headline_point1_dct_description: In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.
rows.label: War of attrition ESS
rows.source_point2_dct_source: John Maynard Smith (1974) The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts
rows.math_point7_skos_notation: with cost linear in time at unit rate and resource value V, the ESS persistence time has density p(x) = \frac{1}{V} e^{-x/V}
rows.record_context: Assumptions: symmetric contests, cost linear in display time, no information about the opponent's choice. Formal status: proved (Maynard Smith 1974); existence and uniqueness in the generalized game proved by Bishop and Cannings (1978).
rows.does_not_establish: not attempted
